title: Ultimate Java Developer Roadmap
description: 22-level structured path from Java fundamentals to production-ready enterprise engineering

levels.title: Java Fundamentals
levels.description: Core syntax, types, control flow, and JVM basics

topics.title: Variables & Data Types
topics.overview: Java is statically typed — every variable has a declared type checked at compile time. Primitives (int, double, boolean) live on the stack; objects live on the heap with references on the stack.
topics.whyItExists: Type safety prevents entire classes of runtime bugs. Explicit types make APIs self-documenting and enable IDE tooling, refactoring, and compile-time validation at scale.
topics.internalWorking: The JVM stores primitives directly in stack frames. Reference types store a pointer (reference) to heap objects. Autoboxing wraps primitives in wrapper classes (Integer, Double) when collections require objects.
topics.realWorldUsage: Payment services use BigDecimal for money (never float). IDs use long/UUID. Feature flags use boolean. Amazon order pipelines validate types at API boundaries before processing.

codeExamples.title: Variables & Data Types — Basic Example
Variables & Data Types — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Prefer long over int for IDs
Declare variables in the smallest scope
commonMistakes: Choosing wrong numeric type causing overflow

interviewQuestions.question: Difference between == and equals()?
interviewQuestions.answer: == compares references for objects, values for primitives. equals() compares logical equality (must be overridden). Always use equals() for String/content comparison.

interviewQuestions.question: Why BigDecimal for financial calculations?
interviewQuestions.answer: float/double use binary floating point causing rounding errors (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3). BigDecimal provides exact decimal arithmetic required for payments.

topics.title: Control Flow & Methods
topics.overview: Control flow (if/else, switch, loops) directs program execution. Methods encapsulate reusable logic with parameters, return types, and access modifiers.
topics.whyItExists: Without structured control flow, code becomes unmaintainable spaghetti. Methods enable decomposition, testing, and the Single Responsibility Principle.
topics.internalWorking: The JVM executes bytecode sequentially. Branch instructions (ifeq, goto) handle conditionals. Method calls push a new stack frame; returns pop it. Switch on String uses hash lookups (since Java 7).
topics.realWorldUsage: Order state machines use switch expressions. Retry loops wrap external API calls. Private helper methods keep service classes under 200 lines at Stripe and Netflix.

codeExamples.title: Control Flow & Methods — Basic Example
Control Flow & Methods — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Keep methods under 20 lines when possible
Use switch expressions over if-else chains
Prefer early returns over deep nesting
commonMistakes: Modifying loop counter inside enhanced for

interviewQuestions.question: Enhanced for vs traditional for loop?
interviewQuestions.answer: Enhanced for (for-each) is read-only over Iterable/array, cleaner syntax. Traditional for gives index control and allows modification. Use for-each by default.

levels.title: Object-Oriented Programming
levels.description: Classes, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation

topics.title: Classes & Objects
topics.overview: Classes are blueprints; objects are runtime instances. Fields hold state, methods define behavior. Constructors initialize object state.
topics.whyItExists: OOP models real-world entities (User, Order, Account). Encapsulation hides internal state and exposes controlled interfaces — essential for large codebases.
topics.internalWorking: new keyword allocates heap memory, invokes constructor, returns reference. Instance fields live in the object; static fields belong to the class. this refers to current instance.
topics.realWorldUsage: Domain models (Product, Transfer, Invoice) are POJOs/entities. DTOs transfer data between layers. Value objects (Money, Email) enforce invariants at construction.

codeExamples.title: Classes & Objects — Basic Example
Classes & Objects — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Use records for immutable value objects
Make fields private, expose via getters
commonMistakes: Anemic domain models with no behavior

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between class and object?
interviewQuestions.answer: A class is a template defining structure and behavior. An object is a concrete instance created at runtime with its own state in memory.

topics.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
topics.overview: Inheritance (extends) reuses parent class behavior. Polymorphism allows treating subclasses as their parent type — enabling runtime method dispatch.
topics.whyItExists: Polymorphism enables plug-in architectures: swap implementations (PaymentProcessor, NotificationSender) without changing client code. Open/Closed Principle depends on it.
topics.internalWorking: JVM uses dynamic dispatch (vtable) for instance methods. At runtime, the actual object type determines which method runs. Static methods and fields are not polymorphic.
topics.realWorldUsage: Payment gateways implement PaymentProcessor interface. Notification channels extend AbstractNotifier. Spring uses polymorphism extensively via @Autowired interfaces.

Inheritance & Polymorphism — Production Pattern

commonMistakes: Using inheritance for code reuse only

interviewQuestions.question: Explain runtime polymorphism with an example.
interviewQuestions.answer: PaymentProcessor p = new StripeProcessor(); p.process(payment) calls Stripe's implementation at runtime despite the interface type. JVM resolves via virtual method table.

levels.title: Collections & Streams
levels.description: Java Collections Framework and functional programming

topics.title: Collections Framework
topics.overview: Java Collections (List, Set, Map, Queue) provide standardized data structures. ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet are the workhorses; choose based on access patterns.
topics.whyItExists: Raw arrays are fixed-size and lack APIs. Collections provide dynamic sizing, iteration, sorting, streaming, and thread-safe variants for enterprise data handling.
topics.internalWorking: ArrayList: dynamic array, O(1) get, O(n) insert middle. HashMap: bucket array + linked list/tree, O(1) average get. HashSet wraps HashMap. Fail-fast iterators detect concurrent modification.
topics.realWorldUsage: HashMap caches product lookups. ArrayList holds order line items. LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order for audit logs. ConcurrentHashMap in multi-threaded caches.

codeExamples.title: Collections Framework — Basic Example
Collections Framework — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Specify initial capacity for large collections
Choose ConcurrentHashMap for shared mutable state
commonMistakes: Wrong Map implementation for use case

interviewQuestions.question: HashMap vs TreeMap?
interviewQuestions.answer: HashMap: O(1) average, no ordering. TreeMap: O(log n), sorted by key. Use HashMap for general lookup; TreeMap when sorted iteration needed.

interviewQuestions.question: How does HashMap handle collisions?
interviewQuestions.answer: Same bucket: linked list (Java 8+) converts to red-black tree when bucket size exceeds 8. Uses hashCode() for bucket, equals() for key match.

topics.title: Streams & Optional
topics.overview: Streams provide declarative data processing (filter, map, reduce). Optional eliminates null checks by wrapping possibly-absent values.
topics.whyItExists: Imperative loops are verbose and error-prone. Streams enable parallel processing and readable pipelines. Optional makes absence explicit in APIs.
topics.internalWorking: Streams are lazy — intermediate ops build a pipeline, terminal ops trigger execution. Optional is a container with isPresent(), orElse(), map(), flatMap(). Never use get() without isPresent().
topics.realWorldUsage: Transform order DTOs to responses. Aggregate revenue by category. Optional.orElseThrow for repository lookups. Parallel streams for batch processing (use carefully).

codeExamples.title: Streams & Optional — Basic Example
Streams & Optional — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Use Optional as return type, not field/parameter
Avoid parallel streams for small data
Use collect with downstream for grouping

interviewQuestions.question: Intermediate vs terminal stream operations?
interviewQuestions.answer: Intermediate (filter, map) return Stream and are lazy. Terminal (collect, forEach, reduce) trigger execution and produce result or side effect.

levels.title: Exception Handling & I/O
levels.description: Error handling, file I/O, and NIO

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.overview: Exceptions signal error conditions. Checked exceptions must be declared/handled; unchecked (RuntimeException) propagate freely. try-catch-finally and try-with-resources manage cleanup.
topics.whyItExists: Errors happen — network failures, invalid input, DB timeouts. Structured exception handling separates error paths from happy paths and ensures resource cleanup.
topics.internalWorking: throw creates exception object and unwinds stack until catch matches. try-with-resources calls AutoCloseable.close() automatically. Suppressed exceptions track errors during close.
topics.realWorldUsage: @ControllerAdvice maps exceptions to HTTP responses. Custom exceptions (OrderNotFoundException) carry error codes. Retry logic catches transient failures.

codeExamples.title: Exception Handling — Basic Example
Exception Handling — Production Pattern

interviewQuestions.question: Checked vs unchecked exceptions?
interviewQuestions.answer: Checked (IOException): compiler enforces handling. Unchecked (RuntimeException): optional handling. Use checked for recoverable external failures; unchecked for programming errors.

topics.title: File I/O & NIO
topics.overview: java.io provides stream-based I/O; java.nio offers channels, buffers, and memory-mapped files for high-performance I/O.
topics.whyItExists: Services read config files, write logs, process CSV imports, and stream large files. NIO enables non-blocking I/O critical for high-throughput systems.
topics.internalWorking: Streams are byte/char oriented. NIO uses ByteBuffer and Channels. Files.readString/writeString (Java 11+) simplify file ops. Path API replaces File class.
topics.realWorldUsage: Load application.yml at startup. Export transaction reports to CSV. Process bulk imports with BufferedReader. NIO for log aggregation pipelines.

codeExamples.title: File I/O & NIO — Basic Example
File I/O & NIO — Production Pattern

commonMistakes: Reading entire large file into memory

interviewQuestions.question: NIO vs traditional I/O?
interviewQuestions.answer: Traditional I/O is stream-based, blocking. NIO uses buffers/channels, supports non-blocking and memory-mapped files. NIO better for high-concurrency servers.

levels.title: Generics & Annotations
levels.description: Type safety and metadata-driven programming

topics.title: Generics
topics.overview: Generics add compile-time type safety to classes, interfaces, and methods. Type parameters (T, E, K, V) eliminate casts and catch errors at compile time.
topics.whyItExists: Before generics, collections stored Object requiring casts and risking ClassCastException at runtime. Generics move type checking to compile time.
topics.internalWorking: Type erasure removes generic info at runtime — List<String> becomes List. Wildcards (? extends T, ? super T) provide flexibility. PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
topics.realWorldUsage: Repository<T, ID> base classes. ApiResponse<T> wrappers. Event handlers with typed payloads. Generic mappers between DTO and entity.

codeExamples.title: Generics — Basic Example
Generics — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Use bounded wildcards for API flexibility
Prefer List<T> over T[] for generics

interviewQuestions.question: What is type erasure?
interviewQuestions.answer: Compiler removes generic type parameters at runtime. List<String> and List<Integer> both become List. Enables backward compatibility but limits runtime type introspection.

topics.title: Annotations & Reflection
topics.overview: Annotations add metadata to code (@Override, @Entity, @Autowired). Reflection inspects and manipulates classes at runtime — fields, methods, annotations.
topics.whyItExists: Frameworks (Spring, JPA, JUnit) use annotations for declarative configuration. Reflection enables dependency injection, ORM mapping, and test discovery without boilerplate.
topics.internalWorking: Annotations are interfaces extending Annotation. Retention policy controls lifecycle (SOURCE, CLASS, RUNTIME). Reflection API: Class.forName(), getDeclaredMethods(), setAccessible().
topics.realWorldUsage: @RestController defines API endpoints. @Transactional manages DB transactions. @Test discovers test methods. Custom @Audited triggers logging aspects.

bestPractices: Create custom annotations for cross-cutting concerns

Prefer compile-time annotation processors when possible

interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring find @Autowired fields?
interviewQuestions.answer: At startup, Spring scans classpath, uses reflection to find @Component classes, inspects fields/constructors for @Autowired, and injects matching beans from the ApplicationContext.

levels.title: Multithreading & Concurrency
levels.description: Threads, executors, and concurrent collections

topics.title: Threads & Executors
topics.overview: Threads enable concurrent execution. ExecutorService manages thread pools, avoiding manual thread creation/destruction. CompletableFuture composes async operations.
topics.whyItExists: Modern services handle thousands of concurrent requests. Thread pools reuse threads efficiently. Async processing prevents blocking I/O from stalling the entire application.
topics.internalWorking: Each thread has its own stack. ExecutorService maintains a work queue and thread pool. CompletableFuture chains async stages with thenApply, thenCompose, allOf.
topics.realWorldUsage: Parallel API calls to payment + inventory + shipping. @Async methods in Spring. Batch job processing with fixed thread pools. CompletableFuture for timeout handling.

codeExamples.title: Threads & Executors — Basic Example
Threads & Executors — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Size pools based on workload (CPU vs I/O bound)

interviewQuestions.question: Difference between Thread and ExecutorService?
interviewQuestions.answer: Thread: manual lifecycle, expensive creation. ExecutorService: managed pool, work queue, reuse, graceful shutdown. Always prefer ExecutorService in production.

topics.title: Concurrent Collections & Locks
topics.overview: java.util.concurrent provides thread-safe collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) and locks (ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, Semaphore).
topics.whyItExists: Standard collections fail under concurrent modification. synchronized blocks are coarse-grained. JUC provides fine-grained, high-performance concurrency primitives.
topics.internalWorking: ConcurrentHashMap uses segment/bucket locking. ReentrantLock supports tryLock, fairness, conditions. volatile ensures visibility. AtomicInteger provides lock-free CAS operations.
topics.realWorldUsage: ConcurrentHashMap for in-memory rate limiters. ReadWriteLock for cache read-heavy workloads. CountDownLatch for service startup coordination. Semaphore for connection pooling.

codeExamples.title: Concurrent Collections & Locks — Basic Example
Concurrent Collections & Locks — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Prefer JUC collections over synchronized wrappers

interviewQuestions.question: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety?
interviewQuestions.answer: Bucket-level locking (not whole map). Reads mostly lock-free. Writes lock only affected bucket. Java 8+ uses synchronized first node or tree bin.

levels.title: JVM Internals & Performance
levels.description: Memory model, GC, and JVM tuning

topics.title: JVM Memory Model
topics.overview: The JVM divides memory into heap (objects), stack (method frames), metaspace (class metadata), and native memory. Understanding this layout is essential for debugging memory issues.
topics.whyItExists: Memory leaks and OOM errors are the #1 production incidents in Java services. Knowing where objects live helps diagnose GC pressure, stack overflows, and metaspace exhaustion.
topics.internalWorking: Stack: local variables, one per thread. Heap: Eden + Survivor + Old gen for objects. Metaspace stores class definitions (replaced PermGen in Java 8). TLAB (Thread Local Allocation Buffer) optimizes allocation.
topics.realWorldUsage: Heap dumps analyzed with Eclipse MAT at Netflix. Stack traces debug infinite recursion. Metaspace tuning for apps with dynamic class loading (Spring, Hibernate).

codeExamples.title: JVM Memory Model — Basic Example
JVM Memory Model — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Set -Xms equal to -Xmx to avoid resize pauses
Use object pooling only when profiled necessary
commonMistakes: Setting heap too large (long GC pauses)
Creating unnecessary object allocations in hot loops

interviewQuestions.question: Stack vs Heap in JVM?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stack: thread-local, stores frames/primitives/references, LIFO, fast. Heap: shared, stores objects, GC-managed, slower allocation. StackOverflow vs OutOfMemoryError.

topics.title: Garbage Collection & Tuning
topics.overview: GC automatically reclaims unreachable objects. Collectors (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) trade throughput vs latency. Tuning minimizes pause times for SLA-critical services.
topics.whyItExists: Manual memory management causes bugs. GC pauses directly impact p99 latency. Financial and e-commerce systems require sub-100ms GC pauses.
topics.internalWorking: Mark-and-sweep identifies reachable objects. Generational hypothesis: most objects die young. G1 divides heap into regions, collects incrementally. ZGC targets <10ms pauses.
topics.realWorldUsage: G1GC default for Java 17+. ZGC for ultra-low latency trading systems. GC log analysis with GCeasy/Grafana. Tuning after load testing, not before.

codeExamples.title: Garbage Collection & Tuning — Basic Example
Garbage Collection & Tuning — Production Pattern
codeExamples.code:
# Kubernetes pod with GC tuning
env:
  - name: JAVA_OPTS
    value: "-Xms1g -Xmx1g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100"

bestPractices: Choose collector based on latency requirements
Tune after load testing with realistic data
Monitor GC pause times in dashboards

interviewQuestions.question: How does G1 GC work?
interviewQuestions.answer: Divides heap into equal regions. Tracks garbage per region. Prioritizes regions with most garbage. Mixed collections reclaim old gen incrementally. Targets pause time goal.

levels.title: Design Patterns
levels.description: Gang of Four patterns and enterprise patterns

topics.title: Creational & Structural Patterns
topics.overview: Creational patterns (Factory, Builder, Singleton) control object creation. Structural patterns (Adapter, Decorator, Facade) compose objects into larger structures.
topics.whyItExists: Direct new() couples code to concrete classes. Patterns decouple creation from usage, enable testing with mocks, and simplify complex object construction.
topics.internalWorking: Factory Method: subclass decides object type. Builder: step-by-step construction with fluent API. Decorator: wraps object adding behavior. All rely on composition and interfaces.
topics.realWorldUsage: Builder for complex Order/Config objects. Factory for PaymentProcessor selection. Decorator for caching wrappers. Spring BeanFactory is a sophisticated factory.

codeExamples.title: Creational & Structural Patterns — Basic Example
codeExamples.code:
Order order = Order.builder()
    .customerId(123L)
    .items(List.of(item1, item2))
    .shippingAddress(address)
    .build();

codeExamples.title: Creational & Structural Patterns — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Use Builder for objects with 4+ parameters
Avoid singleton abuse — use Spring scope
Apply patterns to solve real problems, not speculatively

interviewQuestions.question: Builder vs Factory pattern?
interviewQuestions.answer: Factory: creates different types via common interface. Builder: constructs complex single object step-by-step. Use Builder for many optional params; Factory for type selection.

topics.title: Behavioral & Enterprise Patterns
topics.overview: Behavioral patterns (Strategy, Observer, Command) manage algorithms and communication. Enterprise patterns (Repository, DTO, Saga) address distributed system challenges.
topics.whyItExists: Business rules change frequently. Strategy enables swapping algorithms. Saga manages distributed transactions. Repository abstracts data access from domain logic.
topics.internalWorking: Strategy: interface + multiple implementations, selected at runtime. Observer: publish-subscribe via event listeners. Saga: sequence of local transactions with compensating actions.
topics.realWorldUsage: Strategy for pricing rules (discount, bulk, loyalty). Observer via Spring ApplicationEvent. Saga for order→payment→inventory in CommerceX. Repository pattern in every Spring Data app.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the Saga pattern.
interviewQuestions.answer: Manages distributed transactions as sequence of local TXs. Each step has compensating action. On failure, previously completed steps are undone. Used in microservices instead of 2PC.

levels.title: Spring Framework Core
levels.description: IoC, DI, AOP, and Spring context

topics.title: IoC & Dependency Injection
topics.overview: Inversion of Control transfers object creation to a container. Dependency Injection provides dependencies from outside rather than objects creating them internally.
topics.whyItExists: new ConcreteClass() creates tight coupling and makes testing impossible. IoC enables swapping implementations, mocking in tests, and configuration-driven wiring.
topics.internalWorking: Spring ApplicationContext scans @Component classes, resolves @Autowired dependencies by type/name, manages bean lifecycle (singleton by default), and injects via constructor/setter/field.
topics.realWorldUsage: Every Spring Boot service uses constructor injection. @MockBean in tests replaces real dependencies. @Profile switches implementations per environment.

interviewQuestions.question: Constructor vs Field injection?
interviewQuestions.answer: Constructor: immutable, testable, required deps explicit, recommended. Field: uses reflection, hides dependencies, harder to test. Always prefer constructor injection.

topics.title: AOP & Spring Context
topics.overview: Aspect-Oriented Programming separates cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions) from business logic. Spring Context is the IoC container managing all beans.
topics.whyItExists: Scattering logging/security/transaction code across every method violates DRY. AOP centralizes these concerns. ApplicationContext provides enterprise services beyond basic DI.
topics.internalWorking: AOP uses proxies (JDK dynamic or CGLIB). @Aspect classes define @Before/@After/@Around advice on pointcuts. ApplicationContext adds event publishing, resource loading, i18n over BeanFactory.
topics.realWorldUsage: @Transactional is AOP — Spring wraps methods in TX boundaries. @Cacheable adds caching proxy. Custom @Audited aspect for compliance logging. Context events for startup hooks.

interviewQuestions.question: Why doesn't @Transactional work on self-invocation?
interviewQuestions.answer: Spring AOP uses proxies. this.method() calls target directly, bypassing proxy. Fix: inject self, use AspectJ compile-time weaving, or extract to separate bean.

topics.title: Spring Boot Fundamentals
topics.overview: Spring Boot auto-configures Spring applications based on classpath dependencies. Starters bundle common dependencies. Embedded servers enable standalone JARs.
topics.whyItExists: Spring XML configuration was verbose and error-prone. Boot reduces boilerplate to near-zero, enabling microservices that start in seconds with sensible defaults.
topics.internalWorking: @SpringBootApplication = @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan. Auto-config classes in META-INF/spring apply conditionally (@ConditionalOnClass). Actuator exposes health/metrics endpoints.
topics.realWorldUsage: Every microservice starts as spring init + dependencies. spring-boot-starter-web for REST. spring-boot-starter-data-jpa for DB. Actuator for K8s health probes.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?
interviewQuestions.answer: Scans META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. Each config class uses @ConditionalOn* annotations. Applies only when matching classes/properties exist on classpath.

topics.title: Configuration & Profiles
topics.overview: Externalized configuration via application.yml/properties. Profiles (dev, staging, prod) activate environment-specific settings. @ConfigurationProperties binds typed config objects.
topics.whyItExists: Hardcoded config prevents environment promotion. 12-factor app mandates config in environment. Profiles enable one codebase deployed everywhere with different settings.
topics.internalWorking: Property resolution: command line > env vars > application-{profile}.yml > application.yml. @ConfigurationProperties validates and binds prefix groups. @Profile conditionally loads beans.
topics.realWorldUsage: application-prod.yml with RDS endpoints. SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod in K8s. @ConfigurationProperties for KafkaSettings, RedisConfig. Vault/AWS Secrets Manager for sensitive values.

Configuration & Profiles — Production Pattern

  kafka:

    topic: order-events

interviewQuestions.question: Property resolution order in Spring Boot?
interviewQuestions.answer: Command line args > SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON > ServletConfig > JNDI > System properties > OS env vars > application-{profile}.properties > application.properties. Higher priority wins.

topics.title: REST Principles & Controllers
topics.overview: REST uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resource URLs. Controllers map requests to handler methods returning JSON via @RestController.
topics.whyItExists: REST is the standard for microservice communication. Stateless HTTP enables caching, load balancing, and horizontal scaling. Uniform interface simplifies client integration.
topics.internalWorking: DispatcherServlet routes requests to @RequestMapping methods. HttpMessageConverter serializes/deserializes JSON. @PathVariable extracts URL params, @RequestBody deserializes JSON body.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX catalog API: GET /products, POST /orders. FinFlow: POST /transfers. Versioning via /api/v1 prefix or Accept header. HATEOAS links in mature APIs.

bestPractices: Use proper HTTP methods and status codes

interviewQuestions.question: PUT vs PATCH?
interviewQuestions.answer: PUT: replaces entire resource (idempotent). PATCH: partial update of specific fields. Use PUT for full updates, PATCH for partial modifications.

topics.title: Validation & OpenAPI
topics.overview: Bean Validation (@NotNull, @Size, @Email) validates request data declaratively. OpenAPI (Swagger) generates interactive API documentation from annotations.
topics.whyItExists: Invalid input is the top cause of 500 errors. Validation at the boundary prevents bad data reaching business logic. OpenAPI enables frontend/backend parallel development.
topics.internalWorking: @Valid triggers JSR-380 validation on @RequestBody. Violations throw MethodArgumentNotValidException. springdoc-openapi scans @Operation, @Schema annotations to generate spec.
topics.realWorldUsage: Validate payment amounts, email formats, required fields at API layer. Swagger UI for QA testing. Generated clients for frontend teams. Contract testing with OpenAPI spec.

interviewQuestions.question: How does @Valid work in Spring?
interviewQuestions.answer: JSR-380 annotations on DTO fields. @Valid on @RequestBody triggers Hibernate Validator. Failures produce BindingResult/MethodArgumentNotValidException with field-level error details.

levels.title: JPA & Hibernate
levels.description: ORM, entity relationships, and query optimization

topics.title: JPA Entities & Relationships
topics.overview: JPA maps Java objects to database tables. @Entity defines models, @OneToMany/@ManyToOne/@ManyToMany define relationships. Hibernate is the default JPA provider.
topics.whyItExists: Raw JDBC is verbose and error-prone. ORM eliminates SQL boilerplate, manages object-relational impedance mismatch, and provides caching and lazy loading.
topics.internalWorking: EntityManager persists/flushes changes. Lazy loading via proxies (Hibernate). Cascade types control related entity persistence. @JoinColumn defines FK mapping.
topics.realWorldUsage: Order→OrderItems (@OneToMany). User→Orders (@OneToMany). Product→Category (@ManyToOne). FinFlow Account→Transactions. Spring Data JPA repositories abstract CRUD.

codeExamples.title: JPA Entities & Relationships — Basic Example
JPA Entities & Relationships — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Equals/hashCode on ID only for entities

interviewQuestions.question: Lazy vs Eager loading?
interviewQuestions.answer: Lazy: proxy loaded on access (default, efficient). Eager: loaded immediately with parent (can cause N+1, memory issues). Always default to LAZY, use JOIN FETCH when needed.

topics.title: Query Optimization & Transactions
topics.overview: Optimize JPA queries with JPQL, native SQL, projections, and fetch joins. @Transactional manages ACID properties with propagation and isolation levels.
topics.whyItExists: N+1 queries destroy performance at scale. Wrong transaction boundaries cause data corruption. Proper query design and TX management are critical for financial systems.
topics.internalWorking: Persistence context tracks entity changes. flush() syncs to DB. @Transactional creates proxy wrapping method in TX. Propagation controls nested TX behavior. Isolation prevents dirty reads.
topics.realWorldUsage: JOIN FETCH for order+items in one query. @Modifying for bulk updates. READ_COMMITTED for most services. REQUIRES_NEW for audit logging. Pessimistic lock for inventory.

codeExamples.title: Query Optimization & Transactions — Basic Example
Query Optimization & Transactions — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Use @EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH to avoid N+1
Choose isolation level based on requirements
commonMistakes: N+1 from lazy loading in loops
Wrong propagation causing nested TX issues

interviewQuestions.question: Explain @Transactional propagation REQUIRES_NEW.
interviewQuestions.answer: Suspends current TX, creates new independent TX. Commits/rollbacks independently. Used for audit logs that must persist even if outer TX rolls back.

levels.title: SQL & Database Design
levels.description: Relational design, indexing, and migrations

topics.title: Database Design & Normalization
topics.overview: Relational database design organizes data into normalized tables (1NF→3NF) eliminating redundancy. Primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints enforce integrity.
topics.whyItExists: Poor schema design causes data anomalies, update conflicts, and query performance issues. Normalization ensures consistency; strategic denormalization optimizes reads.
topics.internalWorking: 1NF: atomic columns. 2NF: no partial dependencies. 3NF: no transitive dependencies. FK constraints enforce referential integrity. Indexes speed lookups at cost of write performance.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX: products, categories, orders, order_items tables. FinFlow: accounts, transactions, ledger_entries. Separate read replicas for reporting queries.

codeExamples.title: Database Design & Normalization — Basic Example
codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
  total DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

codeExamples.title: Database Design & Normalization — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Plan indexes based on query patterns

interviewQuestions.question: When would you denormalize?
interviewQuestions.answer: When read performance critical and joins expensive. Examples: storing computed totals, duplicating customer name in orders for display. Always measure before denormalizing.

topics.title: Indexing & Query Plans
topics.overview: Indexes accelerate data retrieval. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals query execution plans. B-tree, hash, and GIN indexes serve different access patterns.
topics.whyItExists: Full table scans fail at millions of rows. Proper indexing reduces query time from seconds to milliseconds. Query plan analysis prevents production slowdowns.
topics.internalWorking: B-tree index: default, good for equality and range. Composite index: column order matters (leftmost prefix rule). EXPLAIN shows seq scan vs index scan, cost estimates.
topics.realWorldUsage: Composite index on (status, created_at) for order listing. Partial index on active users only. Covering indexes avoid table lookups. pg_stat_statements for slow query detection.

codeExamples.title: Indexing & Query Plans — Basic Example
codeExamples.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 123 AND status = 'PAID'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Look for: Index Scan vs Seq Scan, actual rows, execution time

codeExamples.title: Indexing & Query Plans — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Index columns in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY
commonMistakes: Not analyzing after large data changes

interviewQuestions.question: What is a covering index?
interviewQuestions.answer: Index containing all columns needed by query. Database reads only index, not table (index-only scan). Example: index on (customer_id, status, created_at) covers a filtered sorted listing query.

levels.title: Microservices Architecture
levels.description: Service decomposition, boundaries, and communication

topics.title: Service Decomposition
topics.overview: Break monoliths into microservices bounded by business capabilities. Each service owns its data, deploys independently, and communicates via APIs or events.
topics.whyItExists: Monoliths become unmaintainable at scale. Microservices enable team autonomy, independent scaling, technology diversity, and fault isolation.
topics.internalWorking: Domain-Driven Design identifies bounded contexts. Each context becomes a service with its own DB. API gateway routes external requests. Event bus for async communication.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX: user, catalog, cart, order, payment, inventory, notification services. FinFlow: account, transfer, fraud, compliance services. Strangler fig pattern for migration.

codeExamples.title: Service Decomposition — Basic Example
Service Decomposition — Production Pattern
codeExamples.code:
# CommerceX service boundaries
user-service:       users, auth, profiles
 catalog-service:    products, categories, search
cart-service:       cart state (Redis)
order-service:      order lifecycle, saga
payment-service:    payment processing
inventory-service:  stock management

bestPractices: Decompose by business capability, not technical layer
Start with a modular monolith if unsure

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide service boundaries?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use Domain-Driven Design bounded contexts. Each context has its own ubiquitous language, data, and team. Services should change independently. If two domains always change together, they may belong together.

topics.title: Inter-Service Communication
topics.overview: Microservices communicate via synchronous REST/gRPC or asynchronous messaging (Kafka). Each pattern has trade-offs in coupling, reliability, and complexity.
topics.whyItExists: Services must coordinate without shared memory. Communication patterns determine system resilience, latency, and consistency guarantees.
topics.internalWorking: Sync REST: request-response, tight coupling, simple. gRPC: binary protocol, streaming, faster. Async messaging: loose coupling, eventual consistency, buffering during outages.
topics.realWorldUsage: REST for user-facing queries. gRPC for internal high-throughput calls. Kafka for order events, inventory updates. Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures.

interviewQuestions.question: Sync vs async communication?
interviewQuestions.answer: Sync: immediate response needed, simpler debugging, tighter coupling. Async: fire-and-forget, buffering, loose coupling, eventual consistency. Use async for events; sync for queries needing immediate data.

levels.title: Spring Cloud

topics.title: Service Discovery & Config
topics.overview: Service discovery (Eureka, Consul) registers service instances dynamically. Centralized config (Spring Cloud Config) manages settings across environments.
topics.whyItExists: In K8s/cloud, service instances are ephemeral with dynamic IPs. Hardcoded URLs fail. Centralized config enables changing settings without redeployment.
topics.internalWorking: Services register on startup with discovery server. Clients query registry for healthy instances. Config server serves property files from Git. Bus refresh propagates changes.
topics.realWorldUsage: Eureka in Spring Cloud Netflix stack. K8s DNS replaces Eureka in cloud-native setups. Spring Cloud Config with Git backend. Vault for secrets.

bestPractices: Use K8s service discovery in cloud deployments
commonMistakes: Config server as single point of failure
Stale registry entries without health checks

interviewQuestions.question: Eureka vs Kubernetes service discovery?
interviewQuestions.answer: Eureka: application-level, client-side load balancing, Spring Cloud integration. K8s: DNS-based, built-in, no extra infra. Prefer K8s DNS in cloud-native; Eureka for hybrid/on-prem.

topics.title: API Gateway & Circuit Breakers
topics.overview: API Gateway is the single entry point routing, authenticating, and rate-limiting requests. Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures by stopping calls to failing services.
topics.whyItExists: Clients shouldn't know about internal service topology. Gateway centralizes cross-cutting concerns. Circuit breakers provide fault tolerance in distributed systems.
topics.internalWorking: Spring Cloud Gateway routes by path to downstream services. Filters handle auth, logging, rate limiting. Resilience4j circuit breaker: CLOSED→OPEN→HALF_OPEN states based on failure rate.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX gateway routes /products→catalog, /orders→order-service. JWT validation at gateway. Rate limiting per API key. Circuit breaker on payment service calls.

codeExamples.title: API Gateway & Circuit Breakers — Basic Example
API Gateway & Circuit Breakers — Production Pattern

commonMistakes: Gateway becoming a god service with business logic

interviewQuestions.question: Explain circuit breaker states.
interviewQuestions.answer: CLOSED: normal operation. OPEN: failures exceeded threshold, calls fail fast. HALF_OPEN: test call allowed after wait period. Success→CLOSED, failure→OPEN. Prevents cascade failures.

levels.title: Apache Kafka
levels.description: Event streaming, producers, consumers, and schemas

topics.title: Kafka Fundamentals
topics.overview: Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Producers publish to topics; consumers subscribe in consumer groups for parallel processing.
topics.whyItExists: Services need decoupled, reliable, ordered event delivery. Kafka handles millions of events/sec with durability, replay capability, and horizontal scaling.
topics.internalWorking: Topics partitioned for parallelism. Each partition ordered. Consumer groups: one consumer per partition. Offsets track read position. Replication factor ensures durability.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX: order.created, inventory.reserved, payment.completed topics. FinFlow: transaction.events for audit trail. Event-driven order saga orchestration.

codeExamples.title: Kafka Fundamentals — Basic Example
Kafka Fundamentals — Production Pattern

interviewQuestions.question: How does Kafka ensure ordering?
interviewQuestions.answer: Ordering guaranteed within a partition only. Messages with same key go to same partition. Use customerId/orderId as key for per-entity ordering. Cross-partition ordering not guaranteed.

topics.title: Event Sourcing & CQRS
topics.overview: Event Sourcing stores state changes as immutable events. CQRS separates read models (queries) from write models (commands) for optimized access patterns.
topics.whyItExists: Traditional CRUD loses history. Event sourcing provides audit trail, temporal queries, and replay capability. CQRS optimizes read and write independently.
topics.internalWorking: Commands generate events stored in event store. Aggregate rebuilt by replaying events. Projections build read models from events. Snapshots optimize replay for long streams.
topics.realWorldUsage: FinFlow account ledger: every debit/credit is an event. Account balance computed from events. Separate read DB optimized for transaction history queries.

codeExamples.title: Event Sourcing & CQRS — Basic Example
Event Sourcing & CQRS — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Use for domains needing audit trail
Implement snapshots for long event streams
Version your events for schema evolution
commonMistakes: CQRS without clear read/write optimization need

interviewQuestions.question: When to use Event Sourcing?
interviewQuestions.answer: When audit trail required (finance, healthcare). When temporal queries needed (state at point in time). When event-driven architecture natural. Not for simple CRUD with no history requirements.

levels.title: Redis & Caching
levels.description: Caching strategies, session management, rate limiting

topics.title: Caching Patterns
topics.overview: Caching stores frequently accessed data in fast storage (Redis, in-memory) to reduce database load and latency. Patterns: cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind.
topics.whyItExists: Database queries at scale become bottlenecks. Caching reduces latency from 50ms to <1ms. Essential for product catalogs, session data, and rate limiting.
topics.internalWorking: Cache-aside: app checks cache, on miss loads DB and populates cache. TTL controls expiry. Invalidation on writes prevents stale data. Cache stampede mitigated with locking.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX: product catalog cached 15min. Cart stored entirely in Redis. Session tokens with TTL. Rate limiting counters. FinFlow: fraud score cache.

codeExamples.title: Caching Patterns — Basic Example
Caching Patterns — Production Pattern

commonMistakes: Cache stampede on popular key expiry

interviewQuestions.question: Cache-aside vs read-through?
interviewQuestions.answer: Cache-aside: app manages cache (check cache→DB→populate). Read-through: cache layer loads from DB on miss automatically. Cache-aside gives app more control; read-through simplifies app code.

topics.title: Redis Data Structures
topics.overview: Redis provides Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Streams, and more. Each structure optimizes different access patterns beyond simple key-value.
topics.whyItExists: Different use cases need different data models. Sorted sets enable leaderboards. Streams provide lightweight messaging. Hashes store object fields efficiently.
topics.internalWorking: All structures in-memory with optional persistence (RDB/AOF). Single-threaded execution (per shard in cluster). Pub/Sub for messaging. Lua scripts for atomic operations.
topics.realWorldUsage: Strings: session tokens. Hashes: cart items. Sorted Sets: leaderboards, rate limiting windows. Streams: lightweight event log. Sets: unique visitor tracking.

bestPractices: Use Redis Cluster for horizontal scaling
commonMistakes: Using String when Hash is more efficient

interviewQuestions.question: Redis persistence: RDB vs AOF?
interviewQuestions.answer: RDB: point-in-time snapshots, compact, may lose recent data. AOF: logs every write, more durable, larger files. Use both for maximum durability. RDB for backups, AOF for durability.

levels.title: Spring Security
levels.description: Authentication, authorization, OAuth2, and JWT

topics.title: Authentication & JWT
topics.overview: Authentication verifies identity; JWT (JSON Web Token) provides stateless, signed tokens containing claims. Spring Security integrates both for secure APIs.
topics.whyItExists: Microservices can't share server sessions. JWT enables stateless auth where any service validates tokens independently using shared public key.
topics.internalWorking: Login validates credentials, issues signed JWT (header.payload.signature). Each request sends Bearer token. Resource server validates signature and expiry. Refresh tokens enable long sessions.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX user login returns access+refresh tokens. API gateway validates JWT. FinFlow MFA adds second factor. Token expiry: 15min access, 7d refresh.

codeExamples.title: Authentication & JWT — Basic Example
Authentication & JWT — Production Pattern

bestPractices: Never store secrets in JWT payload
commonMistakes: Storing sensitive data in JWT claims

interviewQuestions.question: JWT vs session-based auth?
interviewQuestions.answer: Session: state on server, easy revocation, harder to scale. JWT: stateless, scales horizontally, harder to revoke. Use JWT for microservices with short expiry + refresh tokens.

topics.title: OAuth2 & RBAC
topics.overview: OAuth2 delegates authorization to identity providers. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions via roles (ADMIN, USER, MERCHANT).
topics.whyItExists: Users shouldn't share passwords with third-party apps. OAuth2 enables 'Login with Google' securely. RBAC enforces least-privilege access in enterprise systems.
topics.internalWorking: Authorization Code flow: redirect to IdP, exchange code for token. Scopes limit access. RBAC: User→Roles→Permissions. @PreAuthorize checks roles at method level.
topics.realWorldUsage: FinFlow OAuth2 for partner API access. CommerceX merchant vs customer roles. @PreAuthorize('hasRole(ADMIN)') on admin endpoints. Keycloak as identity provider.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain OAuth2 Authorization Code flow.
interviewQuestions.answer: Client redirects user to IdP login. IdP returns auth code to callback URL. Client exchanges code for access token (server-side). Most secure flow for web/mobile apps.

levels.title: Docker & Kubernetes
levels.description: Containerization and orchestration

topics.title: Docker & Containerization
topics.overview: Docker packages applications with dependencies into portable containers. Dockerfile defines build steps; docker-compose orchestrates multi-container local environments.
topics.whyItExists: Works on my machine problems plague teams. Containers ensure identical environments from dev to prod. Immutable infrastructure enables reliable deployments.
topics.internalWorking: Dockerfile layers cached for fast rebuilds. Multi-stage builds separate build and runtime. Containers share host kernel, isolated via namespaces/cgroups.
topics.realWorldUsage: Each CommerceX microservice has a Dockerfile. docker-compose.yml runs full stack locally. Distroless/eclipse-temurin JRE images for minimal attack surface.

codeExamples.title: Docker & Containerization — Basic Example
codeExamples.code:
# Multi-stage Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

codeExamples.title: Docker & Containerization — Production Pattern
codeExamples.code:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  order-service:
    build: ./order-service
    ports: ["8084:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
      KAFKA_BROKERS: kafka:9092
    depends_on: [postgres, kafka, redis]

interviewQuestions.question: Docker vs VM?
interviewQuestions.answer: VM: full OS per instance, GBs, minutes to start. Container: shares kernel, MBs, seconds to start. Containers lighter but less isolated than VMs. Use containers for microservices.

topics.title: Kubernetes Orchestration
topics.overview: Kubernetes orchestrates container deployment, scaling, and management. Pods, Services, Deployments, and Ingress manage application lifecycle in clusters.
topics.whyItExists: Managing hundreds of containers manually is impossible. K8s provides self-healing, auto-scaling, rolling updates, and service discovery for production workloads.
topics.internalWorking: Deployment manages ReplicaSets managing Pods. Service provides stable DNS/IP. Ingress routes external traffic. ConfigMap/Secret inject configuration. HPA auto-scales on metrics.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX deployed on EKS with 3 replicas per service. Helm charts package K8s manifests. Liveness/readiness probes via Actuator. HPA scales on CPU/custom metrics.

codeExamples.title: Kubernetes Orchestration — Basic Example
codeExamples.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: order-service
        image: commercex/order-service:1.2.0
        ports: [{containerPort: 8080}]
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080}

codeExamples.title: Kubernetes Orchestration — Production Pattern
codeExamples.code:
# Helm values.yaml
replicaCount: 3
resources:
  requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi}
  limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}
autoscaling:
  enabled: true
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilization: 70

interviewQuestions.question: Deployment vs StatefulSet?
interviewQuestions.answer: Deployment: stateless, interchangeable pods, random names. StatefulSet: stable network identity, ordered deployment, persistent storage per pod. Use StatefulSet for databases, Kafka.

levels.title: AWS Cloud Services
levels.description: EC2, RDS, S3, EKS, and cloud-native patterns

topics.title: AWS Core Services
topics.overview: AWS provides cloud infrastructure: EC2 (compute), RDS (managed DB), S3 (object storage), EKS (Kubernetes), SQS/SNS (messaging), and IAM (access control).
topics.whyItExists: Building and maintaining physical infrastructure is expensive and slow. AWS provides on-demand, scalable, pay-per-use infrastructure with global availability.
topics.internalWorking: VPC isolates network resources. IAM roles grant service permissions without keys. RDS handles backups, patching, failover. S3 stores objects with 99.999999999% durability.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX on EKS with RDS PostgreSQL. Product images in S3. SQS for async processing. CloudFront CDN for static assets. IAM roles for service-to-service auth.

codeExamples.title: AWS Core Services — Basic Example
codeExamples.code:
# Terraform RDS
resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  engine         = "postgres"
  instance_class = "db.r6g.large"
  allocated_storage = 100
  multi_az       = true
  backup_retention_period = 7
}

interviewQuestions.question: RDS vs self-managed PostgreSQL on EC2?
interviewQuestions.answer: RDS: managed backups, patching, failover, monitoring. EC2: full control, lower cost at scale, you manage everything. Use RDS for most workloads; EC2 for special requirements.

topics.title: Cloud-Native Architecture
topics.overview: Cloud-native apps exploit cloud elasticity: microservices, containers, dynamic orchestration, and managed services. Designed for resilience, observability, and automation.
topics.whyItExists: Traditional architectures can't scale with demand spikes or survive infrastructure failures. Cloud-native patterns enable 99.99% availability and elastic cost optimization.
topics.internalWorking: 12-Factor App principles guide design. Immutable infrastructure: replace, don't patch. Horizontal scaling via stateless services. Managed services reduce operational burden.
topics.realWorldUsage: CommerceX: stateless services on EKS, managed RDS/Kafka/ElastiCache. Auto-scaling for Black Friday traffic. Multi-AZ deployment. Infrastructure as Code with Terraform.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the 12-Factor App principles?
interviewQuestions.answer: Key ones: config in environment, treat backing services as attached resources, stateless processes, port binding, disposability (fast startup/shutdown), logs as event streams, admin as one-off processes.

levels.title: CI/CD & DevOps
levels.description: Pipelines, GitOps, and infrastructure as code

topics.title: CI/CD Pipelines
topics.overview: CI/CD automates build, test, and deployment. Continuous Integration merges code frequently with automated tests. Continuous Delivery deploys to production reliably.
topics.whyItExists: Manual deployments are error-prone and slow. CI/CD enables teams to ship multiple times daily with confidence through automated quality gates.
topics.internalWorking: Pipeline stages: checkout→build→unit test→integration test→security scan→deploy staging→smoke test→deploy prod. GitHub Actions/Jenkins/GitLab CI orchestrate stages.
topics.realWorldUsage: Platform Engineering project provides reusable GitHub Actions templates. Every PR triggers build+test. Merge to main deploys to staging. Tag release deploys to production.

codeExamples.title: CI/CD Pipelines — Basic Example
codeExamples.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: {java-version: '21', distribution: 'temurin'}
      - run: ./mvnw verify
      - run: docker build -t app:${{ github.sha }} .

codeExamples.title: CI/CD Pipelines — Production Pattern
codeExamples.code:
deploy:
    needs: build
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - run: helm upgrade --install order-service ./charts/order-service
          --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }}
          --namespace production

bestPractices: Fast feedback: unit tests under 5 minutes

interviewQuestions.question: CI vs CD difference?
interviewQuestions.answer: CI: automatically build and test on every commit. CD (Continuous Delivery): always deployable, manual prod trigger. CD (Continuous Deployment): automatic prod deployment after tests pass.

topics.title: GitOps & IaC
topics.overview: GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth for infrastructure and deployment. IaC (Terraform/Pulumi) defines cloud resources in version-controlled code.
topics.whyItExists: Manual infrastructure changes cause drift and outages. GitOps provides audit trail, rollback via git revert, and automated reconciliation by operators like ArgoCD.
topics.internalWorking: Terraform plan/apply creates AWS resources from HCL files. ArgoCD watches Git repo, syncs K8s manifests to cluster. PR review process for all infrastructure changes.
topics.realWorldUsage: Platform Engineering: Terraform modules for VPC, EKS, RDS. ArgoCD deploys Helm charts from Git. Environment promotion via branch strategy (dev→staging→prod).

codeExamples.title: GitOps & IaC — Basic Example

kind: Application

spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/org/commercex-k8s
    path: charts/order-service
    targetRevision: main
  destination:

    namespace: production

commonMistakes: Terraform state not in remote backend
No PR review for infra changes

interviewQuestions.question: GitOps vs traditional CI/CD deployment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Traditional: CI pipeline pushes to cluster. GitOps: cluster pulls from Git (reconciliation loop). GitOps provides continuous reconciliation, easier rollback (git revert), and drift detection.

topics.title: Testing Strategy
topics.overview: Testing pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, minimal E2E tests. Tools: JUnit 5, Mockito, TestContainers, RestAssured. TDD writes tests before code.
topics.whyItExists: Untested code breaks in production. Testing pyramid balances coverage with speed. Unit tests run in milliseconds; E2E tests catch integration issues.
topics.internalWorking: Unit: mock dependencies, test single class. Integration: @SpringBootTest with TestContainers for real DB/Kafka. Contract: verify API agreements between services. E2E: full user journey.
topics.realWorldUsage: 80% unit (Mockito), 15% integration (TestContainers), 5% E2E. Pact for consumer-driven contracts. Mutation testing with PIT for critical payment logic.

bestPractices: Use TestContainers over H2 for integration tests
Run tests in CI on every PR

interviewQuestions.question: Mock vs Stub vs Fake?
interviewQuestions.answer: Mock: verifies interactions (verify calls). Stub: returns canned responses. Fake: working implementation (in-memory DB). Use mocks for behavior verification; fakes for integration tests.

topics.title: Observability Stack
topics.overview: Observability = Metrics + Logs + Traces. Prometheus/Grafana for metrics, ELK/Loki for logs, Jaeger/Zipkin for distributed tracing. Enables debugging production systems.
topics.whyItExists: Microservices create complex failure paths. You can't debug what you can't see. Observability provides the three pillars to understand system behavior in production.
topics.internalWorking: Metrics: time-series counters/gauges scraped by Prometheus. Logs: structured JSON aggregated by Loki/ELK. Traces: OpenTelemetry spans showing request flow across services.
topics.realWorldUsage: Micrometer exports metrics to Prometheus. Grafana dashboards for SLA monitoring. Structured logging with correlation IDs. OpenTelemetry traces across CommerceX services.

interviewQuestions.question: Metrics vs Logs vs Traces?
interviewQuestions.answer: Metrics: aggregated numbers over time (request rate, error %). Logs: discrete events with context. Traces: request journey across services with timing. Use all three together for full observability.
